stops.name: Arizona State Capitol
stops.teaser: A small capitol building that ended up smaller than its architect dreamed.
stops.map: Arizona State Capitol Museum, 1700 W Washington St, Phoenix, AZ
stops.clue: Go to West Washington Street near 17th Avenue. Look for the stone building with a small dome on top, set back behind a lawn.
stops.safety: Washington Street is busy. Use crosswalks, stay on the paths, and check museum hours before you go inside.

q.hint: Think of a desert postcard, and a tree with a tall, bare trunk.

now.head: Today
now.label: The capitol today
now.line: The old capitol, now a museum, with newer government buildings nearby.

story: The Arizona Territory's capital moved around: Prescott, Tucson, Prescott again, and finally Phoenix in 1889. To show the territory was ready for statehood, voters approved a $100,000 bond to build a real capitol.

Architect James Riely Gordon won a design contest. His original plan had wings for the legislature and a big dome, but money was short, so the wings were dropped and a small metal top was used. The capitol was finished in 1900.

Arizona became a state in 1912, and the building became the state capitol. Today the 1900 building is the Arizona Capitol Museum, and newer buildings behind it hold the legislature and the governor's offices.
stops.fact: The capital moved around three times before landing here.
stops.disputed: Some people think Phoenix was always the capital. Wikipedia says the capital started in Prescott in 1864, then moved to Tucson, Prescott again, and Phoenix in 1889.

claims.t: The Arizona Territory's capital moved to Phoenix in 1889.
claims.why: Wikipedia: the legislature voted on January 29, 1889.

claims.t: The capitol was built after Arizona became a state in 1912.
claims.why: It was built in 1900 as the territorial capitol.

spot.q: The 1908 photo shows the capitol with palms and a dirt road. The architect's original plan had wings and a big dome. What happened to them?
options: They were built, then torn down in 1912
Voters asked for a plain flat roof
Money was short, so the wings were dropped and a small metal top was used
spot.why: Money ran short, so the wings were dropped and a small metal top replaced the big dome. The building was finished in 1900.

stops.name: Rosson House
stops.teaser: A bright Victorian house in the middle of a desert city, built by a mayor who quit.
stops.map: Rosson House Museum, 113 N 6th St, Phoenix, AZ
stops.clue: Go to Heritage Square downtown, at 6th and Monroe Streets. Look for a red brick Victorian house with a pointed corner tower.
stops.safety: Heritage Square is downtown, near busy streets. Use crosswalks, check museum hours, and stay on the paths.

q.hint: Walk around it and count the flat faces that go all the way round.
q.verify: Wikipedia describes the tower as French and octagonal. Count the sides on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

now.head: Today
now.label: The house today

story: Dr. Roland Lee Rosson was a doctor and a politician who came to Phoenix in 1879. His house was built between 1894 and 1895 in the Stick-Eastlake Queen Anne style, designed by San Francisco architect A. P. Petit. Petit died in the month it was finished.

Rosson was elected mayor of Phoenix on May 7, 1895, but after trouble with the city council he resigned on April 6, 1896. The house changed hands many times before the City of Phoenix bought it and restored it.
The house mixes styles from different cultures, including a Chinese moon gate, Italian hooded windows and a French octagonal turret. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1971.
stops.fact: Its architect died the month it was finished.
stops.disputed: Some sources say the design is unique. Wikipedia says nearly identical plans appear in an earlier house-plan book.

claims.t: Dr. Rosson was elected mayor of Phoenix in 1895.
Rosson served as mayor for ten years.
claims.why: He resigned on April 6, 1896, less than a year later.

spot.q: The 1940 photo shows the Rosson House, now a museum. Who was Dr. Roland Lee Rosson?
options: A railroad owner from San Francisco
A doctor and politician who became Phoenix mayor in 1895
The architect who designed the house
spot.why: He was a doctor and politician, elected mayor on May 7, 1895. He resigned on April 6, 1896. The architect was A. P. Petit.

stops.name: Arizona Biltmore
stops.teaser: A fancy resort made of patterned blocks, and a famous architect who didn't design it.
stops.map: Arizona Biltmore, 2400 E Missouri Ave, Phoenix, AZ
stops.clue: Go to 24th Street and Missouri Avenue, north of downtown near Camelback Road. Look for a resort made of patterned golden blocks.
stops.safety: The resort is private property. Look from public areas, ask staff before wandering, and watch for cars on the entrance road.

story: The Arizona Biltmore opened on February 23, 1929. Brothers Warren and Charles McArthur built it with hotelier John McEntee Bowman. Three crews worked around the clock to finish it.

Many people say Frank Lloyd Wright designed it. Wikipedia says the architect was Albert Chase McArthur, who had been a draftsman for Wright. Wright consulted for four months in 1928 on the patterned "textile block" system.

Clark Gable and Carole Lombard often stayed here, and the Tequila sunrise was invented here. In 1930 the McArthurs lost control of the hotel, and chewing gum magnate William Wrigley Jr. later became the full owner.
stops.fact: Three crews worked day and night to finish it.
stops.disputed: The big debate: Wright or McArthur. Wikipedia says McArthur is the architect, with original drawings and a 1929 article to prove it.

claims.t: Frank Lloyd Wright was the hotel's architect of record.
claims.why: Albert Chase McArthur was; Wright only consulted.

spot.q: Many people say Frank Lloyd Wright designed the Biltmore. Who does Wikipedia say the architect was?
spot.why: Albert Chase McArthur, who had been a draftsman for Wright. Wright consulted for four months in 1928 on the patterned textile block system.

stops.name: Arizona Falls
stops.teaser: A waterfall that wasn't natural, in a desert, that lit up a city.
stops.map: Arizona Falls, 56th St and Indian School Rd, Phoenix, AZ
stops.clue: Go to the Arizona Canal near 56th Street in the Arcadia neighborhood. Follow the canal path to the little park where water drops over a ledge.
stops.safety: Stay on the canal path and park paths, and watch for bikes. Do not climb on the walls or into the water. It gets very hot, so bring water.

q.hint: It is taller than a person, but shorter than a tall tree.
q.verify: Wikipedia says the canal crosses a natural 20-foot drop. Estimate on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

now.head: Today
now.label: The falls today

story: In 1883, workers began digging the Arizona Canal to bring water to farms in the Valley. In 1884 they hit hard rock at a natural drop of about 20 feet. They left it in place and let the water pour over it, making a waterfall in the desert.

The falls became a popular spot. The mist cooled the air, trees gave shade, and families from Phoenix and Tempe came for picnics. In 1901 and 1902 the Phoenix Light and Fuel Company built a power plant here to provide the first electricity to Phoenix.

After about 50 years of making power, the site was neglected. In the early 2000s it was rebuilt as a public-art project and a working power station that makes enough electricity for about 150 homes. The modern park opened in 2003.
stops.fact: The falls was made by a canal, not a river.
stops.disputed: Many people assume the falls is natural. Wikipedia says it formed when a man-made canal crossed a natural drop.

claims.t: The first power plant here opened around 1901 and 1902.
The waterfall is on a natural river.
claims.why: It formed where the man-made Arizona Canal crosses a natural drop.

spot.q: The old power plant in the photo was built in 1901 and 1902. What was it for?
options: To provide the first electricity to Phoenix
To mill flour for the Valley
spot.why: The Phoenix Light and Fuel Company built it to bring Phoenix its first electricity. The rebuilt station today makes enough power for about 150 homes.
